label: Ordered Geometry
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 175 through 190 and asks how much geometry survives when only incidence and order remain. We keep the primitive predicate of betweenness and discard every measurement of length, angle, area, and curvature, exposing the common nucleus beneath affine and absolute geometry.

label: The Ordered Kernel
notes: Foundational does not mean empty. Absolute geometry adds congruence; affine geometry adds parallel projection; both share the same ordered layer of points, lines, sides, and betweenness. The slide stresses that this kernel already supports segments, rays, separation, and many incidence consequences before any ruler appears.

label: The Betweenness Relation
notes: The single primitive is the relation bracket A B C, read B lies between A and C. The axioms of order govern it: the endpoints are distinct, reversing them fixes the middle point, and bracket A B C excludes bracket B A C. These austere rules are exactly the obvious facts Coxeter insists we name.

label: Segments, Rays, and Lines
notes: From betweenness alone we carve a one-dimensional line into structure. The segment AB is the set of points between A and B; adjoining endpoints gives the interval; the two rays point outward in opposite senses; together the rays and interval reconstitute the entire line without any notion of distance.

label: The Pasch Axiom
notes: Pasch supplies the first major proof engine. A line entering a triangle through one side, missing the vertices, must leave through exactly one of the other two sides. This crossing invariant is a statement about sidedness and order, never about measured lengths, and it cannot be derived from Euclid's earlier postulates.

label: Pasch in Coordinates
notes: A coordinate model keeps the primitive relation visible. Placing E between C and A and extending line DE, we compute its intersection F with side AB and verify F lies strictly inside the open segment. The arithmetic confirms the ordered exit that Pasch's axiom guarantees on purely combinatorial grounds.

label: Triangles and Convex Regions
notes: Sides and betweenness let order define interior and exterior without area. A point is inside a triangle when it lies on the inner side of all three edges, so convex regions arise as intersections of half-planes. Separation of the plane by a line is the engine driving every such region argument.

label: Sylvester's Ordinary Line
notes: Order alone proves a striking incidence fact: any finite, non-collinear set of points admits an ordinary line through exactly two of them. The notebook performs an honest finite search, building every joining line and counting incidences, making the phrase ordinary line concrete before a reader writes the order-based proof.

label: Hyperplanes and Region Counts
notes: Order extends upward through planes and hyperplanes, which slice space into convex cells. In general position m hyperplanes in n dimensions cut a number of regions counted by a sum of binomials obeying a simple Pascal-style recurrence, giving a compact computational check on the separation behavior of arrangements.

label: Continuity and the Dedekind Cut
notes: Density is weaker than continuity. Between any two points lies another, yet rationals approaching the square root of two never supply the boundary itself. A Dedekind cut partitions the line so all of one side precedes the other, and continuity demands that the cut determine a genuine point.

label: Parallelism as Ray Separation
notes: Parallelism is recast without angle. Through a point off a line, rays split into those meeting the line and those missing it, and the boundary directions separate the two fans. Euclidean order yields two parallel directions; the later hyperbolic chapters return here to allow more, distinguishing the parallel axioms.

label: Why Ordered Geometry Matters
notes: Ordered geometry is the shared nucleus from which Euclidean and hyperbolic geometry diverge only when a parallel axiom is chosen. Betweenness, Pasch, separation, and continuity already yield substantive theorems, so the reader sees precisely which ordered claims survive before measurement, coordinates, or curvature are ever introduced.
